facts.title: First Of The Superheavies
facts.text: Rutherfordium, element 104, is the first of the transactinide (superheavy) elements, sitting just past the actinide series. Its discovery marked the start of the 6d transition metals, making it the heaviest element widely treated as a true transition metal. Every atom of it ever made has been produced artificially in a particle accelerator.

facts.title: A Cold War Naming Feud
facts.text: Soviet scientists at Dubna proposed the name 'kurchatovium' (Ku) in 1964 after Igor Kurchatov, while American teams at Berkeley pushed for 'rutherfordium' in 1969. This clash was part of the decades-long 'Transfermium Wars' over priority. IUPAC finally settled the dispute and made 'rutherfordium' official in 1997.

facts.title: Named For The Atom's Father
facts.text: The element honors Ernest Rutherford, the New Zealand-born physicist who discovered the atomic nucleus in 1911 with his famous gold-foil experiment. Fittingly, an element that exists only as fleeting nuclei is named after the man who proved the nucleus exists. Rutherford also won the 1908 Nobel Prize, but in Chemistry, not Physics.

facts.title: Made By Slamming Nuclei Together
facts.text: Rutherfordium is created by fusing lighter nuclei in an accelerator, for example firing carbon-12 ions at californium-249, or neon-22 at plutonium-242. Only a handful of atoms are produced at a time, sometimes just one. The atoms must be detected almost instantly because they vanish within seconds.

facts.title: A Half-Life Of Just Over An Hour
facts.text: The longest-lived known isotope, rutherfordium-267, has a half-life of about 1.3 hours, while most isotopes survive only seconds or less. There are roughly 16 known isotopes, ranging in mass number from about 253 to 270. Because of this fleeting existence, rutherfordium can never be collected as a visible, weighable sample.

facts.title: Chemistry With Single Atoms
facts.text: Scientists study rutherfordium's chemistry one atom at a time using rapid gas-phase and liquid-phase techniques before the atom decays. These heroic experiments confirmed that it behaves like a heavier cousin of hafnium and zirconium, forming compounds such as the volatile chloride RfCl4. It is one of the few elements whose chemistry is explored atom-by-atom rather than in bulk.

facts.title: Relativity Bends Its Behavior
facts.text: In such a heavy atom, inner electrons move at a large fraction of the speed of light, so Einstein's relativity noticeably reshapes the electron orbitals. These relativistic effects can make rutherfordium deviate from the simple predictions of its periodic-table position. Studying it is therefore a real-world test of how relativity influences chemistry.

facts.title: A Predicted Dense Metal
facts.text: No one has ever seen bulk rutherfordium, but calculations predict it would be a solid silvery metal with a density around 17 to 23 grams per cubic centimeter. That would make it roughly twice as dense as lead and comparable to some of the densest known metals. Its expected ground-state electron configuration is [Rn] 5f14 6d2 7s2.

facts.title: It Decays By Splitting Apart
facts.text: Many rutherfordium isotopes disappear through spontaneous fission, literally tearing into two smaller nuclei, while others undergo alpha decay. This behavior near the edge of nuclear stability helps physicists map the limits of how big an atomic nucleus can be. Such studies guide the search for the theorized 'island of stability' of longer-lived superheavy elements.

facts.title: No Role In Nature Or Life
facts.text: Rutherfordium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth and has no known biological role; it exists purely as a product of human-made nuclear reactions. Because only a few atoms are ever made and they decay almost instantly, it has no practical industrial or medical uses. Its sole value is scientific, helping us understand the structure of matter at the heaviest known extreme.
